title: Available vs current balance: what can you spend?
dek: Your bank's two balances answer different questions. Check holds and pending items, then account for bills the bank cannot see before spending.
metaDescription: Understand available versus current balance, pending transactions and holds. Use a worked example to avoid counting the same commitment twice.

sources.name: Chase: how transactions post
sources.note: Bank-specific example: pending transactions affect available balance, some transactions are not visible as pending and daytime visibility does not guarantee later payment.

paragraphs: A current balance commonly reflects transactions that have posted, while an available balance reflects what the bank currently makes available after its treatment of holds and pending items. Labels and calculations differ by bank and account. Neither number is a complete spending plan: a future bill or a transaction the bank has not yet received may still need to be covered.

The app shows two numbers, and the larger one is tempting. The problem is not choosing the optimistic balance. It is working out what each number already includes, and what still has to leave the account. Subtracting every pending item again can be just as misleading as ignoring every commitment.

This guide concerns deposit-account balances, not credit-card available credit. It is general organisation guidance, not a prediction that a bank will honour a particular payment. Read your own account terms and contact the bank about unclear transactions, holds or an unexpected balance.

body.heading: Read the label before using the number

left.label: Current or posted balance
items: Often shows transactions that have posted to the account, under the bank's own definitions.
Useful for matching posted activity and statements, but not a guarantee that all committed money is free.

right.label: Available balance
items: Reflects the bank's current availability calculation, which may account for holds and pending activity.
Still needs checking against unposted commitments and the account terms; do not treat it as a guaranteed safe-to-spend amount.

body.heading: Check the balance without double-counting
items: Note which account and balance label you are using, and the time you checked it.
Inspect pending transactions and holds. Establish whether each is already reflected in the displayed available amount.
List outstanding commitments the bank does not yet reflect, such as a bill you still need to pay or a payment not yet presented.
Keep the money needed before your next reliable income available in the appropriate account. Do not include uncertain income as if it has arrived.
Ask the bank about anything you cannot reconcile, especially unfamiliar charges, negative balances or a hold affecting an important payment.

body.heading: A pending item is not a promise about the final result
paragraphs: A pending amount may change, be replaced by a final transaction or disappear from the immediate view. That alone does not tell you that an obligation has been cancelled. Ask the merchant or bank about the relevant transaction rather than relying on its temporary appearance.

In its [posting guidance](https://www.chase.com/personal/checking/overdraft-services/how-transactions-post), Chase says that pending activity affects available balance, that some authorised transactions may not appear as pending, and that daytime display does not guarantee later payment. This is a specific bank's explanation, not a rule copied across every provider.

If your bank includes an overdraft facility or another credit arrangement in what it displays, separate borrowed availability from your own funds. Check the terms, costs and payment consequences. Do not count a lending limit as income or assume that every account displays it in the same way.

body.heading: The bank cannot reserve an intention it has not received
paragraphs: A bill due next week, a cheque not yet presented, or groceries still to buy may not be represented in the number on screen. Your record supplies that missing context. Keep a [monthly bills list](/guides/monthly-bills-list) and review [what is due before direct debits leave](/guides/what-to-check-before-each-direct-debit-date).

An invented example: the app shows enough for an optional purchase, but an annual insurance payment is due before payday and has not reached the bank. The account is not wrong. The spending decision is missing a commitment. For that broader decision, use [how much money is actually safe to spend](/guides/how-much-of-your-money-is-actually-safe-to-spend).

The opposite mistake is reserving the same purchase in three places: it reduced available, it remains in a pending list, and it is also included in an upcoming-bills total. Match individual items before subtracting totals. A more conservative number is not automatically a more accurate one.

body.heading: Ask the bank a question it can answer

items.line: Which transactions or holds are included in my available balance, and what does the current balance mean on this account? I need to understand this specific item before relying on the displayed amount.
This payment is due and the balance display is unclear. What has posted, what is still pending, and which account terms or processing conditions should I check?

items.q: Should I use current or available balance before spending?
items.a: Available balance is often the more relevant immediate availability figure, but check how your own bank defines it. Account separately for commitments not already reflected. Neither balance guarantees a payment will clear or tells you what is affordable after all upcoming needs. Do not automatically subtract pending items twice.

items.q: Why is my available balance lower than my current balance?
items.a: Pending transactions, deposit availability rules or holds may explain a difference, depending on your account. Open the detailed activity and ask the bank about unclear entries. Do not infer that a particular hold has expired, that a merchant was paid or that a deposit is fully usable from the difference alone.

items.q: Does money disappearing from pending mean I can spend it?
items.a: Not necessarily. A pending display can change before the final transaction arrives. Keep your own record of what you authorised and ask the bank or merchant if the status is unclear. Removing an item from a screen is not the same as confirming that the underlying obligation has ended.

body.heading: Use the account number with the rest of the picture
paragraphs: Start with a balance you understand, match the items already represented, and reserve what remains due. You are building a spending decision, not trying to make the banking app show a more reassuring number.

[Personal Finance Companion](/shop/personal-finance-companion) is an optional organiser for the financial information you enter. It cannot decide what your bank will pay or make an uncertain balance reliable. The worksheet here works without connecting a bank account or buying a product.
